records.title: Street dogs and access to care
records.description: Dogs are living on Stockton's streets. We don't know how many need help, what happens to them, or whether available services are reaching them.
records.central_question: What happens to dogs on Stockton's streets, and what prevents them from getting the care they need?
records.purpose: Understand the conditions dogs face, trace what happens when people seek help, and identify practical ways to improve access to care.

hero.headline: How can we improve care for dogs on Stockton's streets?
hero.subtitle: How many need help? What care is available? Who's providing it? What's preventing more dogs from getting the care they need?

records.summary: Public reports describe roaming and abandoned dogs in Stockton. Animal Services reports shelter-capacity pressure, and organizations report feeding, fostering, and placement work. The number of dogs currently on the streets, their conditions, what happens after someone seeks help, and how reliably care reaches them remain unverified.
what_we_are_seeing: Stockton Animal Services reports recurring shelter-capacity pressure. It prioritizes sick, injured, aggressive, and confirmed abandonment cases, while healthy stray intake generally requires an appointment. Its guidance cautions that a roaming dog may be lost or owned rather than abandoned.
Stockton Street Dogs reports feeding and outreach on the streets several times a week. Its public materials also describe fostering, adoption, and other rescue pathways.

At an October 19, 2026 committee meeting, city officials discussed shelter limitations and repeated roaming-animal violations. The committee advanced proposed animal-control changes for full City Council consideration; the cited report did not establish a final Council outcome.
On October 20, Crossover requested Animal Services field-call records. They were received by email on November 2; their contents and limitations have not yet been assessed here.

San Joaquin County’s 2024 survey reported that 34% of unhoused respondents had pets. St. Mary’s describes pet-accommodating shelter options, but Crossover has not verified current access or whether people with dogs still face restrictions.
contributing_factors: Limited access to affordable and timely veterinary care
Insufficient foster, rescue, and permanent placement
Shelter restrictions and limited support for people who need to remain with their dogs

records.current_state: Stockton Street Dogs reports that dumped-dog encounters rose from roughly one per week a year ago to about three to ten per week, with District 5 seeing notable activity. Stockton Animal Services reports recurring shelter capacity pressure. The current number of street dogs and how many reach safe placement remain unverified. Stockton Street Dogs is also pursuing a proposed Canine Campus for overflow, veterinary recovery, and volunteer-supported care; it is not yet an operating facility. People with pets may face shelter-access barriers; current access and dog-inclusive capacity remain unverified.
